case: 20-year-old, necrotic tooth, no restoration, no caries — what could the cause be?
followups: Any history of trauma to this tooth, even if minor or not thought of as an injury? — luxation is the commonest cause of pulp necrosis in a virgin tooth without caries or restoration.
Which tooth is it, and does it have any visible discoloration or developmental pitting? — dens invaginatus, palatogingival groove, or dens evaginatus would explain necrosis and change management.
Is there a crack, infraction, or isolated deep periodontal pocket on probing? — these are the next most common cause after trauma and would change the prognosis.

**Differential — most likely first**

---

**1. Previous traumatic dental injury**

- *Fits because:* Twenty years old is squarely within the peak incidence window for traumatic dental injuries; pulp necrosis following luxation or concussion with an intact, unrestored, caries-free crown is the single most common explanation for this presentation in this age group. Patients frequently do not volunteer or recall minor blows, especially remote childhood injuries.
- *Argues against:* No tooth position is stated; anterior teeth are overwhelmingly more affected, so if this is a posterior tooth the prior probability drops substantially. No trauma history is documented, but absence of recall ≠ absence of event.
- *Evidence:* Pulp necrosis risk after luxation injuries is strongly associated with closed apices and the type and severity of displacement [[PMID:3460803]]. A competing-risk cohort found that pulp necrosis occurred in 28% of luxated permanent teeth overall, with intrusion and concomitant crown fracture being the strongest predictors [[PMID:38430349]]. The relationship between pulp canal dimensions (closed apex) and necrosis risk post-luxation is established [[PMID:3460803]].

---

**2. Dens invaginatus (dens in dente)**

- *Fits because:* Dens invaginatus creates a pre-formed, enamel-lined channel that admits oral bacteria directly to pulp tissue without any caries process — the archetypal mechanism for necrosis in an intact tooth. Maxillary lateral incisors are the tooth most frequently affected (65.8% of cases in a large radiographic survey), and a 20-year-old would be well within the age at which untreated Type II/III invaginations progress to necrosis.
- *Argues against:* Requires the affected tooth to be (most likely) a maxillary lateral incisor. Type I — the most prevalent subtype (88.6%) — rarely causes necrosis on its own; Type II/III are responsible for the clinical presentation described but represent only ~11% of cases.
- *Evidence:* Prevalence of dens invaginatus is 7.07% in one large radiographic cohort (10,000 patients), with maxillary lateral incisors comprising 65.8% of affected teeth; Type III (the subtype most likely to cause necrosis without caries) accounted for 1.9% [[PMID:41184566]]. The malformation frequently results in early pulp necrosis due to its complex anatomy [[PMID:10332241]]. A case report documents combined nonsurgical and surgical management of Type III DI in a maxillary lateral incisor with a lateroradicular lesion [[PMID:10379279]]. Guided cavity preparation to selectively treat the invagination while preserving pulp vitality has been described [[PMID:41454423]].

---

**3. Dens evaginatus with fractured or worn accessory cusp**

- *Fits because:* Dens evaginatus produces an accessory cusp or talon cusp that contains a pulp horn extension; as the cusp fractures or attrits, the pulp horn is exposed to oral bacteria with no caries involved, producing a tooth that appears caries-free yet is necrotic. Classic in young patients; bilateral periapical pathology in caries-free premolars has been attributed to this mechanism.
- *Argues against:* Predominantly reported in Asian populations and in premolars; the accessory cusp may have been fractured sufficiently long ago that it is no longer visible and may have been missed on clinical examination. Less common than post-traumatic necrosis globally.
- *Evidence:* Bilateral periapical pathology in caries-free premolars caused by dens evaginatus is documented [[PMID:4528501]]. No systematic review in this evidence base specifically quantifies prevalence rates for dens evaginatus-related pulp necrosis in this age group.

---

**4. Cracked tooth with bacterial ingress progressing to necrosis**

- *Fits because:* A crack that does not involve a restoration can admit bacteria repeatedly over months-to-years and cause pulp death; the crown appears intact. Cracked teeth are well described as a cause of necrosis in otherwise intact teeth, particularly in the 40–49 age group but occurring across all adult ages.
- *Argues against:* Peak incidence for cracked teeth is in older adults (40–49 years in one cohort of 561 patients) where cuspal loading accumulates over restorations [[PMID:41887497]]; at 20 years old and without restorations, crack-induced necrosis is a less likely primary mechanism than trauma or a developmental anomaly. The 15-year survival data for endodontically treated cracked teeth show 55% survival at 15 years, underlining their clinical importance [[PMID:41276249]].
- *Evidence:* A retrospective cohort of 561 cracked teeth found maxillary first molars most affected (37%), with the 40–49 age group most frequently involved [[PMID:41887497]]. Preoperative probing depth is the primary prognostic factor for survival of cracked teeth after endodontic treatment [[PMID:41276249]].

---

**5. Periodontal–endodontic communication (retrograde pulpitis)**

- *Fits because:* Aggressive (generalised) periodontitis can occur in young adults; a deep, narrow periodontal pocket communicating with lateral or accessory canals can deliver bacteria to the pulp retrogradely, producing necrosis in a caries-free tooth.
- *Argues against:* Uncommon at age 20; requires clinically demonstrable attachment loss or a narrow sinus-tract-type probing defect; no periodontal findings are described in this case, making it the least likely cause if charting is normal. The literature on pulpoperiodonal interactions is foundational but predominantly expert-opinion level [[PMID:269259]].
- *Evidence:* No paper in this evidence base addresses retrograde periodontitis as a cause of pulp necrosis specifically in 20-year-old patients with no caries. The pulpoperiodonal interrelationship is described in the foundational literature [[PMID:269259]] but without quantitative outcome data for this presentation.

---

**6. Idiopathic / subclinical cause (including herpes zoster-related necrosis)**

- *Fits because:* After exhausting structural explanations, a small proportion of necrotic teeth have no identifiable portal of entry. Herpes zoster reactivation can cause pulp necrosis in otherwise healthy young individuals, though this is rare.
- *Argues against:* Diagnosis of exclusion only; requires elimination of all structural causes above. No paper in this evidence base addresses viral or ischaemic aetiology of pulp necrosis in caries-free young adults.
- *Evidence:* No paper in this evidence base addresses idiopathic or herpes zoster-related pulp necrosis in this presentation.

---

**What would discriminate**

| Test | Candidate(s) it settles | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Periapical radiograph** (first, immediate) | Dens invaginatus (radiopaque invagination/'tooth within tooth' shadow is pathognomonic); post-traumatic sequelae (widened PDL space, root resorption, pulp canal obliteration, periapical radiolucency); dens evaginatus (pulp horn projection toward occlusal) | Highest information per unit chair-time; near-zero cost |
| **Detailed trauma history** (targeted questioning, sports, assault, falls) | Post-traumatic necrosis | Eliminates or confirms the leading diagnosis in seconds; patients need specific prompting about childhood incidents [[PMID:38430349]] |
| **Transillumination + methylene blue dye + bite test** | Cracked tooth | Transillumination identifies the shadow cast by a crack; bite test reproduces pain on release; recommended by AAE [[PMID:AAE-PS-cracked-tooth]] |
| **CBCT** | Dens invaginatus (Oehlers type classification, extent of invagination, periapical anatomy); cracked tooth (vertical crack extent); dens evaginatus | Indicated when 2D radiograph is inconclusive; ESE recommends CBCT for complex anatomy [[PMID:ESE-QG-2023]]; particularly definitive for DI type classification [[PMID:41454423]] |
| **Full periodontal chart (6-point probing)** | Periodontal–endodontic lesion | A single narrow deep probing defect on one surface suggests a retrograde pathway; normal probing effectively eliminates this candidate |
| **Magnification inspection of crown (loupes or microscope)** | Dens evaginatus (worn or fractured accessory cusp); crack | AAE recommends magnification for cracked tooth diagnosis [[PMID:AAE-PS-cracked-tooth]]; ESE recommends magnification for all endodontic procedures [[PMID:ESE-QG-2023]] |
| **Laser Doppler flowmetry** | Differentiates true necrosis from entities mimicking periapical radiolucency (e.g., periapical cemental dysplasia) | Useful when pulp tests conflict with radiographic appearance [[PMID:10348523]] |

---

**Management**

Obtain a periapical radiograph and a detailed trauma history immediately — these two steps will resolve the differential in most cases. If dens invaginatus is confirmed on imaging, CBCT is warranted to classify the type before treatment planning, as Type IIIa may allow selective treatment of the invagination with pulp preservation [[PMID:41454423]], while Type IIIb typically requires conventional root canal treatment combined with surgical management [[PMID:10379279]]. If post-traumatic necrosis is confirmed (the most likely cause), standard non-surgical root canal treatment is indicated; prognosis depends on the presence and size of periapical pathology, with success rates exceeding 96% in necrotic teeth without periapical radiolucency and approximately 86% where a periapical lesion is present [[PMID:2084204]]. If a crack is identified, prognosis is guided by preoperative probing depth — teeth with probing depths below 4 mm have 10-year survival rates of 76% [[PMID:41276249]].
